 $1 Billion, 733 Days: Inside Social Security’s Improper-Payment Backlog
 Opinion
 A Social Security inspector general found $1 billion in improper SSI payments tied to earnings alerts left unresolved for two years. Here’s what went wrong.
 JJ Gouin/Getty Images
 By Jose Navarro Oct 23, 2026 Jose Navarro Jose Navarro is a contributor for The Fulcrum, a nonpartisan publication dedicated to strengthening democracy by fostering informed civic engagement and elevating diverse perspectives. See More Writings by author Social Security's inspector general opened its books this week and found a number that should stop any controller cold: roughly $1 billion in improper Supplemental Security Income payments, made to 333,800 recipients, sitting on top of a backlog the agency has known about for years. The cause was not a hacker, not a sophisticated fraud ring, and not a policy loophole. It was an earnings alert nobody closed out.
 Here is how the mechanism actually works, and why it matters more than the headline figure. When a recipient's reported earnings change, the Social Security Administration's system generates an alert flagging that the payment amount may need adjustment. An employee is supposed to resolve that alert, verify the wage documentation, and correct the payment before the gap compounds. The inspector general's office pulled a sample of 100 such cases. Only 20 had been resolved. Sixty-three had gone untouched entirely, left pending for an average of 733 days, just over two years. Seventeen more were marked "cleared" without the wage documentation ever being fully verified, meaning the case was closed on paper while the underlying question remained open.
 Multiply that failure rate across the full caseload and the agency's own auditors landed on 417,291 recipients with alerts still pending, and roughly $1 billion in resulting overpayments — $344 million of it still recoverable, and $664 million gone for good under the administrative finality rules that bar the agency from clawing back money once too much time has passed. That second figure is the one a controller would flag first. It is not merely money the government failed to collect. It is money the government forfeited its own legal right to ever collect, because the paperwork sat too long.
 Put the number in context. The SSI program pays out $5.8 billion a month to roughly 7 million recipients, many of them elderly, disabled, or with no other income. A $1 billion improper-payment figure is a rounding error against annual outlays in the hundreds of billions, and that is precisely the trap: individually forgivable, structurally significant, and consequent, cycle after cycle, on the same unresolved bottleneck. Michelle Anderson, the assistant inspector general for audit who signed the report, put it plainly: the agency "has the opportunity to strengthen its controls to ensure employees timely and accurately resolve earnings alerts." That is auditor-speak for "someone stopped doing their job, and nobody noticed for two years."
 This is where the story becomes bipartisan rather than partisan, and that is worth saying explicitly. Nobody designed a policy to let $664 million walk out the door permanently. No administration, no party, no piece of legislation set out to create a 733-day queue. This is what happens when a caseload grows faster than the staff assigned to work it, and when a backlog becomes background noise rather than a crisis, because it never generates a single dramatic headline of its own. It simply accretes, report after report, until an inspector general adds it up and the total is substantial enough to notice.
 The agency's own response is instructive, and to its credit, unresisting. SSA agreed to implement all three of the inspector general's recommendations: review and correct the 63 unresolved alerts, review and correct the 17 incomplete verifications, and identify what is actually driving the pattern so it stops recurring. That last item is the one that determines whether this report changes anything. Reviewing the specific 63 cases is a one-time fix. Diagnosing why alerts sit for two years at a time is the only step with any chance of preventing the next inspector general's report from finding the same thing with a different case number attached.
 There is a broader lesson here for how Washington measures accountability. A single agency losing $664 million to its own processing delays will not move a federal budget measured in trillions. But add up every program running the same kind of quietly aging backlog — disability claims, unemployment insurance overpayments, veterans' benefits recalculations — and the aggregate is not a rounding error anymore. It is a pattern of institutions that are diligent about writing rules and much less diligent about enforcing them against their own inertia. A pragmatic fix is not more legislation. It is adequate staffing against the alert queue that already exists, tracked with the same rigor a private-sector controller would apply to any accounts receivable aging past ninety days.
 Congress does not need a new program to address this. It needs an oversight hearing that asks SSA a narrower and more useful question than "how much fraud is there": how many earnings alerts are open right now, how old is the oldest one, and what is the staffing plan to close the gap before the next $1 billion accrues. That is a question with an answer a controller could evaluate in an afternoon. Whether anyone in Washington asks it before the next inspector general's report comes due is the real test of whether this one changes anything.
 Jose E. Navarro , MBA, is a financial controller and founder of The Navarro Report, a public finance and government accountability publication based in San Diego, California.

 Land of the Free, Home of the Capitalism Didn’t Fail America. America Failed to Moderate Capitalism
 Blake Ashby Oct 21, 2026 The signs are everywhere. For many Americans, buying power has improved only modestly despite decades of economic growth. Corporate profits are at an all-time high. We have reached a level of wealth inequality last seen almost a hundred years ago. By many measures, our capitalist economy seems to have failed to deliver broadly shared prosperity. 
 However, the failure isn’t with the free market as an economic approach. Instead, it’s our failure to regulate and moderate the free market, or more accurately, that we have spent 40 years undermining or removing the regulations of the New Deal that made our economy work for more Americans. 
 Almost a century ago our country rejected both socialism, the complete government control of the economy, and unregulated, survival-of-the-fittest capitalism. Instead, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt navigated a middle path between the two, the New Deal. We stayed with capitalism, with the free market, but Roosevelt’s administration implemented a broad range of financial and corporate regulations to ensure our economy worked for more Americans. Using the power of government to moderate capitalism was a fulfillment of the most basic promise of our Constitution, the promise of equality of opportunity. 
 Moderated capitalism had broad support throughout society, and even support from the Republican Party. While they certainly saw the mix differently, Republicans and Democrats agreed that the government should both nurture the free market and make sure it served the whole of our country. 
 And moderated capitalism worked. It allowed us to tap into the immense talent and ambition of every part of our population. Capitalism is more efficient if there is one set of rules; a level playing field allows everyone to compete equally, creating the greatest value for society. Making sure more people shared in that value through reforms like the 40-hour workweek, overtime pay, and unionization put money in people’s pockets and helped create the engine of our massive consumer economy. 
 Our country has backed away from its commitment to moderated capitalism. In part, this happened because of the ebb and flow of history. Our free-market model had won, producing far greater wealth and personal freedom than socialism. Once the Soviet Union collapsed, we stopped paying as much attention. 
 However, most of the blame rests with the two major parties. Both began to step back from, and actively undermine, the compromise of moderated capitalism. The true believers in unfettered capitalism still had a home in the right wing of the Republican Party. They claimed the victory over socialism as their own and argued our economy had matured and needed less regulation. At every opportunity they cast government as inherently incompetent and untrustworthy. Part of the Democratic Party also bought into the idea of “triumphant capitalism,” happily going along with deregulating our economy 
 Page 1 of 2
 while collecting ever larger donations from corporate interests. The Republican Party slowly chipped away at the protections of moderated capitalism, and the Democrats either helped with the dismantling, or stood by and did nothing. 
 As a result, in ways large and small, our country has stepped back from moderated capitalism. We’ve pulled away from using the powers of government to ensure everyone can participate in our economy. We’ve allowed our bridges and roads to slip into disrepair. We’ve retreated from ensuring every student has access to a quality education. We’ve allowed unions to be undermined. We’ve weakened the parts of government that protect us from products that harm us or our environment. We have rolled back financial regulations and consciously chosen not to extend regulation as Wall Street created new financial products, or as new technologies like the Internet were transforming our society. In many different ways, we’ve backed away from our commitment to providing a level playing field. 
 The return of unregulated—even predatory—capitalism has also led to a renewed interest in socialism, in the government takeover of our economy. But the answer still isn’t to abandon the free market—it’s to go back to moderating it. We need to again make sure that every American has the ability and the opportunity to participate in our economic system. We need to get back to one set of financial, investing, and insurance rules. We need to get back to an updated New Deal, to again make our economy work for all Americans. 
 Blake Ashby is author of Socialism and the Democratic Party: The Case for a Return to Moderated Capitalism, President of the Ferguson Democratic Township, and a political consultant working with Democratic candidates.

 The American Dream Needs a New Economic Operating System
 Paul Maglione Oct 21, 2026 It is, by now, not an exaggeration to state that the traditional American Dream—work hard, buy a house, raise a family, and retire securely—is failing. It was built for a labor-based economy in which steadily rising wages allowed ordinary families to accumulate wealth. But America has become an asset-based economy, and ownership of those assets is extraordinarily concentrated.
 Since the 1980s, the returns from capital have far outpaced the returns from labor. Inflation-adjusted wages for ordinary workers have risen only modestly, while the real value of equities has multiplied many times over. Housing, education, healthcare and childcare costs have soared, employment has become less secure, and defined-benefit pensions have largely disappeared. Even two-income households with respectable jobs often struggle to buy a home, build savings and accumulate enough for retirement.
 Meanwhile, the wealthiest 10% of households own roughly 87% of directly and indirectly held corporate equities and mutual-fund shares, as well as approximately two-thirds of total household wealth. The bottom half owns only a small single-digit percentage. Wealth derived from appreciating assets compounds faster—and is frequently taxed more favorably—than wages.
 Hard work still matters, but it is no longer enough. Unless people acquire appreciating, income-producing assets early in life, they may remain financially insecure regardless of how steadily they work. Artificial intelligence, automation, age discrimination and periodic mass layoffs are likely to deepen that insecurity.
 Social Security cannot solve the problem. Declining birth rates mean fewer workers supporting more retirees. Under current projections, the retirement trust fund will become unable to pay scheduled benefits during the 2030s, potentially requiring cuts of more than 20% unless Congress acts.
 America therefore confronts three related problems: the transition from labor-generated prosperity to asset-generated wealth; falling birth rates partly driven by financial insecurity; and a retirement system approaching a funding crisis. A majority excluded from the asset economy will increasingly resent those who benefit from it, intensifying political polarization and making radical redistribution appear attractive.
 Higher taxes and larger transfer programs do not address the underlying dynamic. Nor would Universal Basic Income. UBI would require enormous recurring expenditures while creating no corresponding asset. It treats insufficient income as the problem when the deeper problem is unequal ownership of the capital that generates wealth.
 If America has become an asset-based economy, the logical response is to make asset ownership universal.
 An American Birthright Account
 The recently created “Trump Accounts” point in the right direction by providing eligible children with a $1,000 investment account to which families, employers, and others may contribute. But $1,000 invested at 7% annually would grow to only about $15,000 after 40 years. A meaningful solution must be much larger.
 Suppose every American child received an individually owned Birthright Account at birth, containing $35,000 invested in a diversified portfolio of American stocks and bonds. Assuming a 7% nominal annual return, 2.5% inflation, and low management fees, that account could grow over 50 years to approximately $300,000 in today’s purchasing power—or about $1 million in 2076 dollars.
 The principal could not normally be withdrawn before age 50, and gains would be tax-free once the beneficiary reached that age. Parents, relatives, friends and employers could make additional tax-advantaged contributions. Even $50 a month could add approximately $79,000 in today’s purchasing power after 50 years.
 With roughly 3.6 million births annually, the initial federal investment would be about $126 billion per year, plus modest administration and brokerage costs. This is substantial, but it should not be viewed like Medicaid or another consumption expense. It would be an annual asset purchase: a national investment held in private accounts for American citizens.
 The money would begin working immediately. A permanent annual flow of $126 billion into American securities would provide patient capital to businesses, increase demand for Treasury and corporate bonds, and modestly reduce market volatility. During recessions, the program would continue buying, allowing accounts to acquire more shares at depressed prices.
 Over several decades, the accounts could accumulate trillions of dollars. That capital would belong not to foreign governments, large institutions or a small affluent minority, but to ordinary Americans. After 30 years, the program could hold nearly $12 trillion in nominal assets, making its beneficiaries one of the largest ownership constituencies in corporate America.
 Paying for It
 The program should not be financed by printing money or simply adding to the national debt. Instead, several dedicated sources could be combined.
 First, a U.S. sovereign wealth fund could receive income from federal mineral, oil and gas rights, spectrum auctions, government equity holdings, surplus federal property and federal loan portfolios.
 Second, a 0.01% levy on secondary-market purchases of stocks, bonds, exchange-traded funds and selected derivatives could generate an estimated 30–35 billion annually. It would add only 50 cents to a $5,000 ETF purchase.
 Third, an “AI productivity dividend” could dedicate part of the corporate tax revenue arising from highly automated, exceptionally profitable businesses to the citizens whose employment prospects automation may weaken.
 Fourth, federal research grants could sometimes include small public equity stakes in recipient companies, producing revenue when successful firms go public. Carefully verified reductions in waste, fraud and administrative costs could provide a smaller supplementary share.
 The accounts would require strong statutory protection against political raids, cancellation or diversion. Assets should remain individually owned and professionally managed, with strict custody safeguards. Limited borrowing against a minority of the account might be permitted for a first home or a privately financed business, but the central purpose—creating long-term financial security—must be protected.
 Giving Every American a Stake
 Birthright Accounts would not eliminate inequality. Affluent parents would still provide their children with greater advantages. The proposal would instead close the enormous gap between inheriting assets and beginning adult life with nothing.
 Every American would become an investor at birth and would eventually own a share of the companies whose productivity generates national wealth. That ownership could encourage financial education, entrepreneurship and public support for policies that sustain long-term economic growth. It could also reduce future dependence on Social Security, housing assistance and other transfers.
 Most importantly, the proposal addresses economic inequality at its source. Rather than repeatedly redistributing income after wealth has been created, it distributes ownership of the assets that create wealth in the first place.
 The economy’s operating system has changed. A policy designed for an age when wages reliably produced security can no longer meet the needs of an economy in which capital appreciation increasingly determines who prospers.
 The choice is ultimately straightforward: America can leave future generations an ownership stake in the nation’s productive wealth—or leave them only an increasingly unpayable share of its debt.
 Paul Maglione is an American entrepreneur and writer currently living in Europe. He writes mostly about politics, society, and entertainment.

 What's Good for the Blue Collar Worker is Good for America
 Ronald L. Hirsch Oct 16, 2026 While our culture of consumerism has benefited corporate America, it has harmed our citizens, hurt our economy, and weakened our nation. It has been particularly harmful to the American blue-collar worker, sacrificed to the holy grail of maximizing profit and globalization by America's multinational corporations. America's welfare dep ends on a thriving middle class, on prosperous blue-collar workers .
 How has our consumer economy hurt America? Let me count the ways. 
 Psychologically, mass marketing images have created a nation of individuals who are constantly dissatisfied with their lives … whether it’s how they look, the job they have, how much money they make, the home they live in, etc. No aspect of our lives escapes this need to project success or power/popularity, mostly through acquiring material things. And we always want more; it’s never enough.
 You won’t find evidence of this in satisfaction polls, because our culture places a premium on feeling good and being happy. And since people feel that they’re supposed to feel good and be happy—that state is valued by our culture—people put on that façade … not knowingly but in an act of self-deception. So while satisfaction polls show that the vast majority of people are satisfied now with their lives, studies of depression show that a large percentage of Americans are depressed with their lives, especially youth .
 While I know of no studies that document what I am about to posit, I believe that the large increase in the extent of depression in this country, especially among youth and young adults, stems not from more awareness of life’s problems, as has often been stated, but from this constant dissatisfaction that people feel about themselves, together with the alienating impact of technology. Indeed, when people feel down, it's not uncommon to get a “fix” by going out to buy something or going to their screens.
 Our economy has also become addicted to consumerism. 68% of our GDP is derived from consumer spending. But consumerism is a very unproductive use of the nation’s wealth. It does not move our country forward. 
 And since much of what we consume is no longer produced here but overseas, increased demand for consumer goods doesn’t help employment like it used to—just the opposite. Because corporations can now produce the goods they sell almost anywhere in the world to take advantage of cheaper production costs, the combination of lost jobs and the cudgel of competition of low-cost overseas workers has resulted in the wages of the American blue-collar worker stagnating since the 70s while the cost of living and corporate profits have soared,
 Meanwhile, the United States is falling behind other countries on various measures and entering a dangerous period because we cannot afford to do what it takes to keep this country strong … and I don’t mean military spending. I mean spending on infrastructure, both maintenance and new. I mean spending on education and health care. I mean spending on housing. I mean spending on cutting-edge research and development, investment in new industries that will drive our economy in the future.
 To stop this focus on consumerism and find the money to invest in our country’s wellbeing, we must shift our economy from one based primarily on consumerism to one based primarily on building our country. This involves changing the components of our GDP without reducing it or our growth. On the contrary, because it would mostly involve projects that must, by their very nature, be accomplished within the United States, it would create millions of jobs for American blue-collar workers instead of jobs outsourced overseas. Jobs for American workers in industry and construction would increase significantly.
 To shift from a consumer economy to a nation-building economy, we will need to wean ourselves off the need to constantly buy things to be happy. American industry will have to change much of what it produces, but it proved it could do just that in WWII. Instead of using discretionary income for self-gratification, we will need to get comfortable with that money going to the government in the form of taxes, to fund projects that benefit the nation, and thus ultimately ourselves. This will be a difficult, complicated process and require a commitment over many years.
 Many will howl at the suggestion of higher taxes, but we must remember that the United States has by far the lowest tax rate of any developed country. Yet, and this bears repeating, people in those countries, despite the high taxes, not only prosper but also have a higher level of wellbeing … whether in health, education, or other measures … than Americans do.
 Making such a change in our culture will take principled leadership and preferably a united political front. We must approach this like a war used to be … all hands on deck and united. And everyone must be prepared to sacrifice. 
 At this point in our history, that concept … a united political front … as well as group sacrifice seem impossible to imagine. Yet we must strive toward that end if America is to regain its global strength and provide all its citizens—not just the well-off or rich—with a secure, comfortable standard of living and a sense of well-being.
 The saying used to be, "What's good for General Motors is good for America." That thought was thoroughly debunked many years ago, and as shown again in this article, what is good for corporate America is often not good for the country. But the truth that I present in the title, "What's good for the blue collar worker is good for America," is unassailable because it is in the welfare of the average American that the health and vitality of our country is dependent.
 Ronald L. Hirsch is a teacher, legal aid lawyer, survey researcher, nonprofit executive, consultant, composer, author, and volunteer. He is a graduate of Brown University and the University of Chicago Law School and the author of We Still Hold These Truths . Read more of his writing at www.PreservingAmericanValues.com

 Love Him or Hate Him, Open a Trump Account
 Megan Thiele Strong Sabrina Mendez-Escobar Oct 11, 2026 Last year, Congress established 530A tax-advantaged investment accounts for children under the age of 18. These accounts are now open and eligible children born between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2028 receive a $1000 contribution from the federal government. This August, philanthropists Michael and Susan Dell gave $6.25 billion to supercharge these so-called Trump accounts, $250 goes into the accounts of the first 25 million children who have an account, are 10 and under and live in qualifying zip codes. Two hundred and fifty dollars was deposited into our children’s 530A Trump accounts. 
 However, as of July 2026, less than 10% of children eligible to open an account actually had an account. Too many of those who are economically worst off have not opened these 530a accounts . Research shows that families with higher incomes, older people, men and white people are more likely to be aware of this opportunity compared to families with lower incomes who are younger, women and Black and Latino. Given the historical, persistent racial and growing economic wealth gap, opportunities to build wealth should not be overlooked. 
 Regardless of how we feel about Trump, there are benefits to opening a federal investment account. For many of us, our instincts to most things Trump are eye rolls, deep sighs and gag reflexes. Like us, it might feel blasphemy to open this account. But, as researchers who study child development and stratification, we know that context matters and “it depends” is a legitimate scientific answer. While important questions remain about these accounts, it is possible to open a Trump account without adding any personal contributions. Thus, it makes sense to open one, so as not to leave money on the table.
 In a world where the wealthiest among us are tied to investment accounts and investment in the stock market is highly stratified, expanding access is socially sustainable. Yes, a majority of Americans own some stock ( 62% ), but stock ownership varies substantially by income, race and ethnicity. Lower-income adults are considerably less likely to own stocks ( 28% ) compared to other income groups. And, while 70% of white adults own stock, only 53% of Black adults and 38% of Latino adults own stock.
 Similar stark disparities also play out with 529 plans, one of the best known college savings plans that up to 54% of parents don’t even know exist. Most children do not have a 529 plan and family contribution varies by race and income with wealthy white families being the most invested. California’s ScholarShare 529 tracks its account owners by race and ethnicity. Black account owners make up 1% of their account owners, Latinos 8% . 
 As social and developmental scientists, we consider how factors such as race, ethnicity, and discrimination influence the development and economic circumstance of minoritized children and their families within US society. We understand that so many of these wealth building accounts were not created with Black and Latino families, women, or low-income people in mind, yet these populations have much to gain if these accounts remain stable and grow wealth. 
 To be sure, the outcome of these accounts is unpredictable. Beyond his actions which make him a social pariah to so many, such as the racism, the sexual abuse and his general animosity to anyone who doesn’t prefer and obey him, Trump’s uniquely long track record of failed ventures might be a deterrent . But, if Trump’s detractors are less likely to open an account than those who vote for and support him, then a pathway is set for a President to effectively grow the wealth of mainly his supporters. And, according to United States constitutional law, Trump will not be in office at the end of business January 20th, 2029. Perhaps instead of putting their names on buildings, landmarks, monuments, etc. the next President can change the name of these accounts to a more neutral one. 
 Until then, in these times of such extreme wealth inequity, social instability and racialization, we need to be willing to take what works for us, regardless of our feelings towards any given political actor. We may think Trump is abhorrent, that doesn’t mean we need to deny ourselves a broadly accessible public wealth-building program. It may mean we need to double down on any such crumb.
